backTranslation:
Check rain, frost, heat, soil and water availability at your site before choosing plants.

Mango can be damaged by frost. Quince needs a suitably cold winter in order to bear reliably.

The name of a region or a sheltered corner is not enough. Confirm each plant and each variety with a trusted local guide.

The first list includes pecan, walnut and native fig; apple, pear, plum, black mulberry and loquat; rosemary, Wild Medlar, Cape gooseberry and Barbados cherry.

This list is not a recommendation for all of them. Check each plant against frost, soil, mature size and the local approved species list.

Keep existing legal and project restrictions in force. Do not plant from seeing a photo alone.

First examples for hot areas include mango, avocado, Natal Mahogany, banana, pawpaw, litchi, Wild Fig, Barbados cherry and Wild Dagga.

Marula, Mopane and baobab also appear in the Limpopo examples. Suitability for your site still needs checking.

Useful trees are not automatically edible. Confirm which plant it is and its safe use; a landscape photo is not a guide for identifying food.

Native plants suited to the site can support wildlife habitat as part of the design.

Choose according to your site's ecology and the useful role of each plant. There is no percentage target based on a trusted source in this lesson.

Protect existing natural vegetation. Do not convert living grasslands into a food forest just because the trees are useful somewhere else.
flags: 'Igama lommandla ... ayiyonto' - concord should be 'aliyonto' (igama is class 5); minor
'aluyiyo ingcebiso yazo zonke' - unusual negative copula form ('alulo/asiyo'); meaning recoverable

backTranslation:
Start by checking the site, the water supply and the care available. Protect bare soil early.

Temporary support plants can give shelter and useful cut material where suitable.

Main trees and lower layers can be put in as conditions allow. Ground-cover plants do not need to wait until the end; avoid plants competing with young trees.

Start with an area you can water and maintain. Check existing plants before clearing.

Where suitable, plain cardboard under suitable mulch can reduce unwanted growth. Keep water able to enter the soil and leave tree trunks clear.

Plan spacing by the plants' mature size. Prepare nursery plants for the next suitable planting window.

Look at how shade, roots and existing water affect neighbouring plants.

Comfrey and wild garlic appear in a first understorey planting example; check their suitability for your site before using them.

Cut or reduce support plants when needed, using methods suited to each species. Suitable clean cuttings can go back as mulch. Do not wait for some fixed year if competition is already damaging plants.

Choose a planting time when soil moisture and expected weather support establishment.

Rain can help, but check the root zone and keep a reserve (lit. 'kept') watering plan if needed. Avoid planting into waterlogged soil.

Check young plants after planting. Harvest time and inputs brought in from outside depend on species, site and care; there is no guaranteed harvest in the fifth year.
flags: 'amanzi enokungena' - concord should be 'anokungena' (class 6); minor
'isicwangciso ... esigciniweyo' renders backup as 'kept/stored plan'; approximate
'akukho sivuno siqinisekisiweyo kunyaka wesihlanu' = 'no harvest guaranteed in year five' - check the English scope

backTranslation:
Ask what the buyer wants: product, quantity, quality, delivery and payment date.

Compare market fees, transport, packaging and unsold produce with the selling price.

Check the market rules and local trading and food requirements. An informal stall is not automatically free of rules or costs.

Selling direct can keep a bigger share of the sale price, but it takes time, packaging, transport and customer care.

A box scheme supplies a regular selection of produce frequently to customers who have agreed (lit. 'who agree with each other').

Agree on what goes in the box, price, payment and what happens when crops are scarce. Regular orders help planning only when customers and farmers can keep the agreement.

Start with what you can supply reliably and what customers want.

Check costs and household food needs before promising regular boxes.

Garden size or number of customers alone does not tell you income. Try an arrangement you can manage and record the results.

If produce changes week to week, avoid promising fixed deliveries you cannot supply.

Offer the surplus harvest you have and agree clear terms with buyers.

Describe your farming methods honestly. Check any certificate or claim buyers require before using a label.
flags: 'abathengi abavumelaneyo' literally 'buyers who agree with each other' rather than 'buyers who agreed with you'; minor

backTranslation:
The clip shows cutting a branch: the support tree stays standing. Leave enough healthy leaves for the plant to recover.

Match the cutting to the plant type. Avoid cutting too often on pigeon pea, especially when you grow it to harvest peas.

Mulch protects the surface, helps keep moisture and returns organic material.

Leave a way to reach it for watering and inspection. Cut material into manageable pieces and keep checking moisture and rot.

Get the correct cultivar (selected variety). Bocking 14 does not spread by viable seed, but root pieces can sprout again.

Place it where it has enough room and moisture. Cut leaves as it recovers; do not press/crowd the young fruit tree.

Many ladybirds (small spotted insects) eat aphids (small sap-sucking insects); some parasitoid wasps (bee-like insects that attack other insects) attack pest insects. Flowering plants like African basil can add resources.

Check which insects visit and whether damage changes. A flowering plant does not guarantee pest control.

Tulbaghia violacea has small narrow leaves and pale purple (lilac) flowers. Place the group of plants where it has light and room to grow.

Watch visiting insects. Do not promise that a wild garlic ring will repel pests or cure outbreaks.
flags: Inconsistent 'iinambuzane'/'izinambuzane' spelling (izi- form is Zulu-leaning, though seen in Xhosa)
'ungawuxinezeli' = 'do not pressure/crowd' - check intended English

backTranslation:
Dry seed must be mature before collecting. Remove the chaff (soft waste surrounding the seed) and damaged seed, then finish drying it in shade with moving air.

Seed in fleshy fruit needs a method particular to each crop. Tomato seed can be fermented for a short time to help remove its gel, then rinsed and dried well. Keep the working jar open or loosely covered. Fermentation is not needed for all wet-seeded crops and does not guarantee disease-free seed.

Pollination (transfer of pollen from one flower to another) is also important. Maize pollen is carried by wind, and maize can cross with other varieties. Tomatoes mostly pollinate themselves, but crossing happens. Check the crop and variety before planning isolation or saving seed.
flags: Pollination gloss 'from one flower to another' omits within-flower self-pollination; minor
English loanword 'pollinate' used as verb stem 'zi-pollinate'; acceptable but code-mixed

backTranslation: Tomatoes mostly pollinate themselves but can cross; maize pollen is carried by wind. Check isolation guidance specific to the crop and variety before saving seed.
Maize pollen is carried by wind and maize crosses easily over distance; tomatoes mostly pollinate themselves.
flags: 'emgama' - questionable locative of 'umgama' (expected 'kumgama'/'emgameni' or 'kude'); meaning still guessable

backTranslation:
Dry seed well before storing it: in paper envelopes, not plastic, in a shaded place with moving air - never use direct sun or trapped heat. The three enemies of seed's ability to germinate are heat, light and moisture. Seed life in storage varies by crop and conditions, so test germination before relying on stored seed.

Write on each envelope the crop, variety and the date it was stored. Keep well-dried seed in a closed container in a cool, dark, dry place. Sealing damp seed can trap moisture inside and spoil it.

Before a new planting season, test a small batch by germinating it so that you do not rely on seed that has quietly lost its ability to germinate.

Plan seed swapping with neighbours this season. What one household keeps well, many households can share - and the whole group's diversity of varieties grows with each swap.
flags: 'Oko umzi omnye ukugcina kakuhle' - missing relative suffix (expected 'ukugcinayo'); ungrammatical but understandable
First sentence structure makes it ambiguous whether drying or storing happens in paper envelopes; check English

backTranslation:
Honeybees and other insects carry pollen (lit. 'flower powder') and drop it on other flowers. This helps many fruit and vegetable crops, including avocado. Different crops and varieties differ in what they need for pollination. A beehive does not guarantee a better harvest everywhere: weather, water, plant health and other pollinating insects also matter.

South Africa has two native honeybee subspecies. The Cape honeybee is found in the Western Cape and some parts of the Eastern Cape. The African honeybee is native to central Africa and most of Southern Africa. These natural ranges are generally not a guide for moving bees. The Department's control measures set a dividing line for bee movement. Check the current rules for moving bees with the Department and an experienced local beekeeper before moving bees or hives.

Learn from an experienced local beekeeper before getting a hive. Keep hives away from busy paths, homes and places where children play. Morning sun can help; a safe site matters first. Give bees flowering plants through all seasons of the year and avoid exposing bees to pesticides. Busy (working) bees are not proof that the farm has no chemicals or diseases. National honeybee control measures require registration for specified beekeeping activities, including managed hives for bee products, queen rearing, bringing in pollen by trade (commercial pollination), and removal, destruction or moving of a swarm. Ask the Department if you are not sure whether the rules apply to your activity. If a colony repeatedly goes out in groups (swarms), ask a trained beekeeper to inspect it. Crowding is one possible reason, not a diagnosis of the problem.
flags: 'wezintyatyambo' - Xhosa expects 'weentyatyambo' (Zulu-style izi- vowel); minor
'ukungenisa umgubo ngokurhweba' for commercial pollination is awkward (literally 'bringing in powder by trading')
'iqela leenyosi liphuma ngamaqela' for swarming is awkward
Check the English range of the African honeybee ('central Africa' and 'most of Southern Africa')

backTranslation: A jar test only gives a general idea of soil texture; it is not a complete soil test.

Compost is organic matter decomposed under controlled conditions.

Finished compost can improve soil structure and contributes nutrients.

Time to readiness varies with materials, moisture, air and heat. A province name or a fixed number of weeks is not a test of readiness.

Mix dry browns (dry brown materials) with fresh greens (fresh green materials). Avoid thick, wet layers that block air.

If the heap becomes slimy or smells strongly of ammonia, add dry browns and turn it.

Check moisture and air as the heap changes; one recipe does not suit all mixtures of materials.

A hot middle temperature does not guarantee that every part of the heap has been treated. Time, heat and management all matter.

Do not put meat, milk and dairy products, diseased plants, pet waste and contaminated materials into this simple home system.

Do not assume that home composting destroys all weed seeds or all disease-causing organisms. Use a recognised process where sanitation is required.

Do not put wattle seed pods (lit. 'seed shells') into the compost heap. An ordinary heap may not make all the seed unable to grow.

Use only clean, untreated materials. Tree bark decomposes slowly; being only bark does not guarantee that it cannot be contaminated.

Check the heap and turn it when it needs air or more mixing. Keep it moist rather than waterlogged.
flags: 'amaqokobhe embewu' = 'seed shells/husks' for pods; loanword in brackets carries meaning
'ukuba lixolo kuphela akuqinisekisi ukuba alinakungcola' - check against English (untreated vs uncontaminated)

backTranslation: Do not add seed pods and contaminated materials.
flags: Does not say 'wattle'; check English

backTranslation: Why should wattle seed pods not be put into an ordinary compost heap?
Seed pods release a gas that kills all living things in the soil.
An ordinary heap may not expose all the seeds to conditions that make them unable to grow. Leaving the seed pods out avoids spreading them along with the compost.

A staple crop earns its place because it feeds the household beyond harvest day.

It carries energy or protein. It stores, or it stays in the ground until we need it. And often it carries cultural memory too.

One staple crop leaves you unprotected. Two or more give you choice when weather or pests strike.

Grow at least two. Not one.

Which staple does your household depend on most right now? That is the one that would hurt most if it failed - so that is the one that needs a partner.

Each staple crop protects you against something different.

Maize gives calories, and it stores dry. Open-pollinated maize (its pollen carried naturally by wind or insects) also allows you to save your own seed, if you manage isolation and selection.

Beans and cowpeas give a protein harvest that can be stored.

Sweet potato develops some drought tolerance after storage roots have formed. It needs water in the first weeks and while the roots are forming; water stress at that time can reduce yield. Its young leaves are also edible.

Amadumbe survive in wetter soil, where other staples struggle.

Notice that they fail in different conditions. That is exactly the point.

Resilience does not mean nothing fails.

It means one failure does not end your household's food plan.

One crop is one (single) point of failure.

Two or more staple crops give you more ways to keep eating.

Different crops use water, soil and seasons differently. That difference is protection.
flags: 'Isityalo esinye sisenye indawo yokusilela' - 'sisenye' can read as 'is another' rather than 'is a single'; slightly ambiguous

backTranslation: Tank planning must compare available water and demand in the rainy and dry seasons. A fixed size for one region cannot do that.
It is much more acidic and changes soil pH over time.
